meta.title: Korean Language Mastery Roadmap
meta.subtitle: 16 levels across 6 phases — from Hangeul & phonetics to professional fluency & native mastery

phases.name: Foundations
phases.themeLabel: Hangeul, sound system, survival Korean, grammar engines I & II
phases.goal: Build the substrate everything else sits on: a sound system you can actually produce, a reading system that works on words you have never seen, and the grammar engine that generates sentences instead of storing them. By the end of this phase you read anything aloud correctly, survive a week in Korea without English, conjugate any verb in any tense, and talk about your past for three minutes.
phases.rule: **The rule of this phase:** you do not "know" a pattern until you have produced it out loud, unprompted, in a sentence about your own life. Reading an explanation is preparation for learning, not learning.

dashboard.study commitment: 2–3 hours per day, 6 days per week; the 7th day is a checkpoint
dashboard.core tools: Anki, a recorder, Naver Dictionary, *Korean Grammar in Use – Beginning*, a tutor from L2
dashboard.final outcome: Read at 60+ syllables/min with all sound rules; hold a 3-minute unprepared conversation on your own life; produce 55 grammar patterns; command 700 active words.

levels.title: HANGEUL AND THE SOUND SYSTEM
levels.goal: Read any Korean text aloud correctly — including words you have never seen — with all seven sound-change rules applied without conscious thought. Then produce the sounds well enough that a native speaker does not have to work to understand you.
levels.mainProject: **`sound-lab`** — a recorded corpus proving you can read and pronounce

levels.title: SURVIVAL KOREAN
levels.goal: Survive a week in Seoul with no English. Introduce yourself, order food, buy a ticket, ask directions, apologise, and understand the answer — in polite Korean that does not offend anyone.

levels.title: THE GRAMMAR ENGINE I
levels.goal: Stop memorising sentences and start generating them. By the end you can conjugate any regular verb into any of three tenses, negate four ways, and place every core particle correctly.

levels.title: THE GRAMMAR ENGINE II
levels.goal: Connect clauses into discourse, handle all the irregulars fluently, use honorifics in the full system, and tell a three-minute story about your own life that a native speaker would call fluent.

elements.text: **The brief.** Spend sixty minutes entirely in Korean. No English, no dictionary app, no switching. One conversation, one topic, one hour.

items.text: **Duration.** 55–65 minutes, continuous, with a tutor, an exchange partner, or a native speaker.
**No English.** Zero English words, zero code-switching. If you cannot say something, you must circumlocute — describe it another way.
**Topic coverage.** At least four of: your work or study, your family, your city, a trip you took, a film or book you liked, a plan for next year.
**Grammar coverage.** At least one instance each of: past, present, future, negation (both 안 and 못), a connector, a noun modifier, an honorific sentence.
**Repair.** At least three instances of asking for clarification *in Korean*, and at least one of correcting yourself mid-sentence.
**The recording and the transcript.** Full audio, plus a 15-line transcript of the most and least successful exchanges.
**The retrospective.** Written, in Korean if possible, answering: what did I avoid saying, and what structure would have let me say it?

Natural-speed comprehension, contraction rules, native rhythm

elements.text: Phase 2 assumes Phase 1 completely: you will listen to natives who speak at a speed your grammar cannot yet predict, and you will read texts whose vocabulary you do not have. The foundation is what lets you survive that.
*Phase 1 of 7 · Levels 0–3 of 18 · Foundations*

phases.name: Everyday Fluency
phases.themeLabel: daily life domains, listening & pronunciation mastery, reading & writing
phases.goal: Move from *can form sentences* to *can live in the language*. By the end of this phase you handle housing, banking, hospitals, bureaucracy, phone calls and workplace Korean without preparation; you understand natural-speed everyday speech at 90%; and you read a news brief and write a 300-word diary with correct spacing and register.  **The shift.** Phase 1 taught you to construct. Phase 2 teaches you to *operate*. The grammar stops being new and starts being recombined at speed, in domains where a wrong word has a real consequence — a deposit, a prescription, a deadline.
phases.rule: **The rule of this phase:** every domain must be *performed*, not *studied*. Reading a list of hospital vocabulary is not healthcare Korean. Standing in a room, saying "열이 나고 기침이 나요" to a partner who then asks a follow-up question, is.

dashboard.core tools: Anki, recorder, tutor (weekly, now essential), Naver Dictionary, *Korean Grammar in Use – Intermediate*, graded readers, a news app
dashboard.final outcome: Twelve life domains handled in Korean; native-speed listening at 90%; newspaper headlines read; a 300-word diary and a formal email written correctly.

levels.title: DAILY LIFE DOMAINS
levels.goal: Handle the twelve situations that make up an actual life in Korea. Not tourist Korean — the Korean of a lease, a prescription, a bank transfer, and a phone call from someone who expects an answer.

levels.title: LISTENING AND PRONUNCIATION MASTERY
levels.goal: Close the gap between the Korean you can read and the Korean you can hear. By the end of this level you understand natural-speed everyday speech at 90%, catch the contractions that are never written, recognise the major dialects by ear, and produce rhythm and intonation that no longer sounds translated.

levels.title: READING AND WRITING FOUNDATIONS
levels.goal: Read a news brief and a short story with 90% comprehension; write a 300-word diary, a formal email, and a message thread — each in the correct register, with correct spacing.
levels.mainProject: **`text-lab`** — a reading log, a diary, an email, and an error taxonomy

elements.text: **The brief.** Live one full day in Korean, and document it. Not a day of study — a day of use. From waking to sleeping, every Korean interaction is either real or simulated, and every one is logged.

items.text: **Morning (07:00–09:00).** A two-minute voice note in Korean describing your plan for the day, in future tense.
**A news brief (09:00).** Read one article, skim then close-read, and write a 100-word summary in -다 style.
**A phone call (11:00).** A real or simulated call of 3+ minutes — booking, enquiring, or rescheduling.
**A listening block (14:00).** A 10-minute audio clip, transcribed with an error map and a genre label.
**A conversation (17:00).** Fifteen minutes with a tutor or partner, on a topic neither of you prepared.
**A diary entry (21:00).** 150 words, -다 style, covering the day.
**An evening reflection (22:00).** A five-minute voice note in Korean: what was hard, what you avoided, and what you will practise tomorrow.

elements.text: **Phase 3 — Intermediate Range · Levels 7–9**

rows: quoting others, being acted upon, causing events
해요체 / 합니다체 / 해체 / 반말 without slipping; reading tone

elements.text: Phase 3 is where the language stops being a set of situations and becomes a way of thinking. You will argue, report, hedge, and joke — and the grammar for those is a different order of difficulty from ordering a coffee.
*Phase 2 of 7 · Levels 4–6 of 18 · Everyday fluency*

phases.name: Intermediate Range
phases.themeLabel: discourse & connectors, reported speech & passive/causative, register & nuance
phases.goal: Move from *can handle situations* to *can think in the language*. By the end of this phase you argue a position for five minutes with structure and concession, quote other people accurately with the right hearsay marker, describe events in the passive and the causative, and move between four registers without slipping.  **The shift.** Phases 1 and 2 taught you to survive situations. Phase 3 teaches you to hold a *position* — and the grammar for that is a different order of difficulty. A request is one clause. An argument is a structure: claim, reason, example, concession, conclusion — each with its own ending, and each with a politeness level that has to stay consistent across all five.
phases.rule: **The rule of this phase:** every new form is produced in *three registers* before the block is closed — 해요체, 합니다체, and -다. A pattern you can only use politely is a pattern you cannot use in writing, and vice versa.

dashboard.study commitment: 2–3 hours per day, 6 days per week
dashboard.core tools: Anki, recorder, tutor twice weekly, *Korean Grammar in Use – Intermediate/Advanced*, a debate podcast, a drama with subtitles off
dashboard.final outcome: A five-minute structured argument; accurate reported speech; passive and causative; four registers used without a slip; nuance endings read correctly.

levels.title: DISCOURSE AND CONNECTORS
levels.goal: Hold the floor. Say something for five minutes that has a beginning, three reasons, a concession, and an end — in the right register, without the listener having to work to follow you.
levels.mainProject: **`argument-lab`** — a five-minute argument with a Q&A

levels.title: REPORTED SPEECH, PASSIVE, AND CAUSATIVE
levels.goal: Move other people's words, and change the direction of a verb. By the end you report what someone said with the correct hearsay marker, describe being acted upon without sounding like a translated English sentence, and distinguish the passive from the causative where Korean uses the same suffix for both.
levels.mainProject: **`voice-lab`** — a retelling, a news summary, and a voice audit

levels.title: REGISTER AND NUANCE
levels.goal: Say the same thing four different ways, and know which one a situation demands. By the end of this level you move between 해요체, 합니다체, 해체, and 반말 without a slip, and you can hear the difference between a neutral statement, a reproach, a discovery, and a joke — which in Korean is carried almost entirely by the final ending.
levels.mainProject: **`register-lab`** — one piece of content, four registers

elements.text: **The brief.** Sit on a three-person panel, in Korean, for thirty minutes. Deliver a five-minute opening statement on an assigned topic, take questions, disagree with someone politely, and summarise the discussion at the end — all in the correct register for a semi-formal setting.

items.text: **The opening statement.** Five minutes, structured with the five-part skeleton from 7.6, in 합니다체.
**The Q&A.** Ten minutes, including one hostile question and one you cannot answer.
**The disagreement.** Disagree with another panellist twice, using two different concession patterns, without dropping the register.
**The summary.** Three minutes at the end, summarising the panel's positions — including one you disagree with, reported fairly using quoted speech.
**The register log.** Every register switch, with the trigger.
**The recording and transcript.** Full thirty minutes, with the transcript annotated for structure.
**The reflection.** Written in Korean, 200 words, on what you avoided saying.

elements.text: **Phase 4 — Advanced Grammar and Vocabulary · Levels 10–12**

rows: the TOPIK 4–5 set: supposition, regret, inevitability, hearsay, and forty more
1,800 Hanja roots; decoding unfamiliar words on sight

elements.text: Phase 4 is where vocabulary stops being a list and becomes a system. The grammar at L10 is mostly combination — patterns built from patterns you already have — and L11 is the single largest return on time in the entire roadmap, because it triples your vocabulary without adding cards.
*Phase 3 of 7 · Levels 7–9 of 18 · Intermediate range*

phases.name: Advanced Grammar & Vocabulary
phases.themeLabel: TOPIK 4-5 patterns, 1,800 Hanja roots, idioms, proverbs & plain form
phases.goal: Bridge the gap between upper-intermediate communication and advanced stylistic fluency. In this phase, Korean vocabulary stops being a random memorisation list and transforms into a generative root system via 1,800 Sino-Korean Hanja morphemes; advanced grammar patterns (supposition, regret, inevitability, and hearsay) become subconscious speech habits; and culturally dense idioms (사자성어), proverbs (속담), and mimetic words (의성어·의태어) grant your Korean texture, humour, and expressive authority.
phases.rule: **The rule of this phase:** You do not study vocabulary by memorising isolated headwords. You study the morphemes (roots) that generate them. A learner who knows 300 Hanja roots commands 6,000 words on sight.

dashboard.study commitment: 2–3 hours per day, 6 days per week
dashboard.core tools: Naver Hanja Dictionary, Anki (Sino-Korean root decks), *Korean Grammar in Use – Advanced*, Korean editorial podcasts, language partner
dashboard.final outcome: Sight-decode unfamiliar 3- and 4-syllable Sino-Korean words instantly; produce 80+ advanced grammar patterns without pauses; deploy 50 사자성어 and 30 proverbs in natural argument; write a 1,200-word essay in 해라체 (plain form).

levels.title: ADVANCED GRAMMAR PATTERNS
levels.goal: Master the TOPIK Level 4–5 grammar architecture: multi-clause hypothetical conditions, nuanced supposition, regret, inevitability, and concessive constructions. Transition from "correct sentences" to expressing exact degrees of probability, intention, and emotional stance.

levels.title: THE SINO-KOREAN VOCABULARY ENGINE
levels.goal: Decode 1,800 Hanja roots to unlock exponential vocabulary growth. In this level, polysyllabic Sino-Korean words (which comprise over 60% of modern Korean vocabulary) stop being isolated strings of sound and become transparent morphological compounds.
levels.mainProject: `hanja-lexicon` — personal 300-root cross-reference network decoding 1,500 advanced words

levels.title: IDIOMS, PROVERBS, AND EXPRESSIVE LANGUAGE

levels.mainProject: `expressive-voice` — a 1,200-word published-grade opinion column in 해라체

elements.text: **The Discourse Dossier**

**Goal.** Prove that your Korean has moved past transactional utility into stylistic authority. The phase capstone combines all three levels into an integrated deliverable: an advanced analytical essay and an unprepared 10-minute speech.

items.text: Written entirely in 해라체.
Must demonstrate Level 10 grammar synthesis (at least 15 distinct advanced patterns).
Must utilize Level 11 Sino-Korean vocabulary compounds deconstructed accurately.
Must include at least 6 사자성어 and 3 속담 seamlessly integrated.
Delivered in formal 하십시오체 with spontaneous connectors.
Defend a controversial thesis without reading from a script.
Address 3 hypothetical counterarguments using concessive and hypothetical structures (`-더라도`, `-을망정`, `-느니 차라리`).
Spontaneously produce hypothetical clauses with `-(으)ㄹ 텐데`.
Accurately distinguish `-은 모양이다` from `-나 보다`.
Conjugate without hesitation using `-을 뻔했다` and `-을 걸 그랬다`.
Recognize 300 productive Hanja roots on hearing.
Decode unknown 3-syllable compounds in newspaper headlines on sight.
Explain homophonic distinctions in common pairs (e.g. `전기`, `수도`, `사고`).
Active recall of 40 사자성어 in conversational debates.
Flawless 해라체 plain form consistency in long-form writing.
Mastery of sound symbolism in 의성어/의태어.

phases.name: Specialization
phases.themeLabel: professional Korean, business meetings & negotiations, literature & media
phases.goal: Up to now, every level has been about the language itself. This phase splits it by *purpose*. By the end you can run a meeting, present to a client, negotiate, write a business proposal, and interview in Korean — and you can also read a novel chapter, a journal abstract, and a political editorial with full comprehension.  **The shift.** You are no longer learning Korean. You are learning *two Koreans*: the institutional one and the literary one. They share grammar and diverge almost completely in vocabulary, rhythm, and what counts as a good sentence. A manager's Korean and a novelist's Korean are not the same language spoken at different speeds.  **Why both, even if you only need one.** The professional register is what you use to earn. The literary register is what makes the professional one legible — because newspapers, editorials, and any marketing copy that is any good are written in the literary voice.
phases.rule: **The rule of this phase:** every section produces an artefact that a professional or a reader would recognise as belonging to the genre. A "business email" that reads like a textbook exercise fails, even if every particle is correct.

dashboard.study commitment: 2–3 hours per day, 6 days per week
dashboard.core tools: A real workplace or simulated one, business-writing corpora, a novel, a journal database, two tutors (one professional, one literary)
dashboard.final outcome: A 20-minute presentation, a 3,000-word report, a negotiation, a mock interview, a literary analysis, and an academic abstract written in Korean.

levels.title: PROFESSIONAL KOREAN
levels.goal: Operate inside a Korean organisation. Not "survive a business trip" — function as a colleague: attend and run meetings, present to a room that outranks you, write documents that get approved, negotiate without rupturing the relationship, and interview for a job.
levels.mainProject: **`professional-kit`** — a meeting, a presentation, a proposal, and an interview

levels.title: MEDIA, LITERATURE, AND ACADEMIC KOREAN
levels.goal: Read the Korean that is written to be *read*, not spoken. By the end of this level you read a newspaper editorial and identify its argument, a short story and identify its narrative technique, a journal abstract and extract the method, and a poem and hear what it does with sound — and you can write an abstract and a literary analysis of your own.
levels.mainProject: **`canon-lab`** — an analysis, a translation, and an abstract

elements.text: **The brief.** Produce one professional deliverable and one literary deliverable, both in Korean, both at a standard a Korean professional or an editor would accept — then defend them in conversation.

items.text: **The professional deliverable.** A 2,000-word report or proposal on a real problem, nine-section structure, plus a 10-minute presentation of it.
**The literary deliverable.** A 1,200-word critical essay on a Korean short story, with quoted evidence.
**The translation.** 800 words of the story translated into English, with a translator's note.
**The defence.** A 30-minute recorded interview where a native questions both deliverables: the report's method, the essay's reading.
**The register comparison.** One page contrasting the professional and literary registers, with a quoted sentence from each and an analysis of the difference.
**The reading record.** The full L13–L14 log, with comprehension estimates.
**The error ledger.** 200 entries from this phase, classified by category.

elements.text: **Phase 6 — Precision and Certification · Levels 15–16**

rows: the exam as a skill: format, timing, and the 230/300 score

elements.text: Phase 6 is the first phase with an *external* marker. Everything so far has been judged by a tutor or by you; L15 is judged by a national exam, and L16 by whether a professional would publish your translation. That external standard is why the phase exists.
*Phase 5 of 7 · Levels 13–14 of 18 · Specialization*

phases.name: Precision & Certification
phases.themeLabel: TOPIK II mastery (Levels 5–6), professional translation & interpretation
phases.goal: Two things happen here at once. First, you take the language you already have and make it *measurable* — an externally judged score you can put on a document. Second, you learn a craft that forces you to understand Korean more deeply than fluency ever does: translation.  **The shift.** Everything before this was about *using* Korean. This phase is about *accountability*. A tutor can be generous. An examiner is not. A client is not.  **Why these two belong together.** TOPIK 6 is roughly the level at which professional translation into Korean becomes possible. And translation is the single fastest way to find the exact holes in your grammar that a score of 230 will expose but never explain. The exam tells you that you have a gap. Translation tells you where it is.
phases.rule: **The rule of this phase:** nothing counts until it is scored by someone who has no reason to be kind to you. Self-assessment is allowed everywhere else in this roadmap. Here it is not.

dashboard.final outcome: A timed mock score ≥ 230/300, and a translation portfolio with a consecutive interpretation that a professional would sign their name to.

phases.name: Mastery
phases.themeLabel: native-adjacent fluency, cultural depth, teaching & lifelong maintenance
phases.goal: Close the distance that no exam can measure, and then build the machinery that keeps the language alive for the rest of your life.  **The shift.** Every previous phase added capability. This one removes the last visible seams. There is no new grammar in L17 and almost no new vocabulary. What is left is timing, subtext, humour, cultural reference, and the hundred small choices that make a sentence sound like it came from a person rather than a learner.  **The honest framing.** This is the phase that never ends, and it is the only one that cannot be completed by finishing a file. L17 has a finish line — a native speaker has to forget, for a measurable stretch of time, that you are foreign. L18 has none, because teaching and maintenance are practices, not milestones.
phases.rule: **The rule of this phase:** nothing here can be done alone for long. Every gate in L17 requires a native speaker, and every gate in L18 requires a learner. That is not an accident — it is the design. The last 5% of a language exists only between people.

dashboard.suggested duration: 6–12 months to the L17 pass; then indefinite
dashboard.study commitment: 2 hours per day, but the *shape* changes: less study, more living
dashboard.core tools: Native friends who will not flatter you, a recorder, a class you teach, Korean-language media as a default rather than a study object
dashboard.final outcome: Sixty minutes of unprepared speech, a short story in Korean, a lesson you taught, and a written plan for the next twenty years.

levels.title: NATIVE-ADJACENT FLUENCY
levels.goal: Be mistaken for a native for a sustained stretch — not on the phone for thirty seconds, and not because you said one idiom correctly, but for twenty minutes in a conversation you did not prepare.  **What this level is not.** It is not accent elimination. Some learners reach near-native prosody and some never do, and the difference is mostly age of onset and ear. Accent is the least important thing in this level and the thing learners obsess over most. **Being mistaken for native and being native-adjacent are different targets, and only the second one is required here.**
levels.mainProject: **`fluency-proof`** — a 60-minute unprepared talk, a 3,000-word short story, and a native-blind test

levels.title: TEACHING AND LIFELONG MASTERY
levels.goal: Two things. First, be able to *explain* Korean — which is the deepest test of understanding there is, and the only one that exposes the gaps that fluency hides. Second, build the regime that keeps the language alive for decades, because the single most common outcome of reaching an advanced level is losing it by neglect.  **Why teaching is the final level.** A user of a language can be excellent and still not know why anything works. A teacher must be able to say what the rule is, when it bends, which exceptions matter, and why the learner's version was wrong rather than merely different. That knowledge cannot be faked, and building it fixes things fluency never touched.
levels.duration: 3–6 months to the teaching certification; the maintenance regime is permanent
levels.mainProject: **`the-teacher`** — a taught unit, a diagnosis, a curriculum, and a rubric

elements.text: **The brief.** There is no exam above TOPIK 6, so the capstone is the invention of one: a panel of three native speakers who do not know you well, a day of performance, and a verdict you cannot appeal.  **Why it is called the Passing.** Because the thing being tested is not knowledge. It is whether you can pass — as a colleague, as a conversation partner, as a writer, as a teacher — in front of people with no reason to be generous.

levels.title: HANGEUL AND THE SOUND SYSTEM
levels.goal: Read any Korean text aloud correctly — including words you have never seen — with all seven sound-change rules applied without conscious thought. Then produce the sounds well enough that a native speaker does not have to work to understand you.

dashboard.core tools: Anki, a recorder, a native-speaker audio source, a syllable chart
dashboard.main project: **`sound-lab`** — a recorded corpus proving you can read and pronounce
dashboard.final outcome: 60+ syllables/min on unseen text, correct sound rules, and a phoneme inventory you can produce on demand.

sections.title: Why Hangeul is a design problem, not a memorisation problem

items.text: Every consonant shape encodes where the sound is made: `ㄱ` the tongue rising at the back; `ㄴ` the tongue at the ridge; `ㅁ` the shape of a mouth; `ㅅ` the shape of teeth; `ㅇ` the throat, empty.
Consonants come in families — plain, aspirated, tensed — and the aspiration is drawn *as an extra stroke*: `ㄱ` → `ㅋ`, `ㄷ` → `ㅌ`, `ㅂ` → `ㅍ`, `ㅈ` → `ㅊ`.
Vowels are built from three elements: a dot (sky, ㅗ/ㅏ), a horizontal line (earth, ㅡ), a vertical line (human, ㅣ). Every compound vowel is a combination.
There are no capitals, no cursive, and no positional letter variants.

elements.text: This is why the script is learnable in days. It is one of the few writing systems in the world that a literate adult can acquire analytically rather than by rote.

items.text: It is phonemic, not phonetic: it spells the *morpheme*, not the sound. `꽃이` is written with ㅊ and pronounced [꼬치].
Sound changes are unwritten. The gap between spelling and speech is the whole difficulty of Korean listening.
Spacing (띄어쓰기) carries grammatical information and is a separate skill (L6).

elements.text: **Module completion gate (0.1).** You can explain, in two sentences, why Hangeul is fast to learn and why that does not make Korean fast to learn.

rows: between English *g* and *k*; no puff of air
Spanish *pero* between vowels; *l* as a final
a placeholder at the start of a syllable

items.text: English has a two-way distinction (voiced/voiceless). Korean has three: **plain** (ㄱ), **aspirated** (ㅋ), **tensed** (ㄲ).
Say the triplet `가 / 카 / 까` until a native speaker or a recording confirms all three are distinct.
Do not rely on voicing ([g] vs [k]) — Korean's plain series is voiced between vowels and voiceless elsewhere, which is not a distinction English ears track.
Hold a sheet of paper in front of your mouth: ㅋ and ㅌ should move it, ㄱ and ㄲ should not, and ㄲ should feel tighter in the throat than ㄱ.

elements.text: **Why this matters now.** If you cannot distinguish these three at the start, you cannot hear them later — and Korean is full of minimal pairs that depend on them: `불` fire / `풀` grass / `뿔` horn.
**Module completion gate (0.2).** You produce all nineteen consonants on demand from a random order, and a recording of yourself saying 가/카/까, 다/타/따, 바/파/빠 is audibly three-way different.

rows: teeth together, lips flat, a grunt — **not** *oo*
*bed*, shorter; merged with ㅐ for most speakers under 50
glide; as the possessive particle it is pronounced 에

modules.title: The two collapses to fix now

items.text: **ㅓ vs ㅗ.** English speakers round ㅓ into ㅗ. Say pairs: 어-오, 어-오. Then `언어` (language) — it must not become 오노.
**ㅡ vs ㅜ.** ㅡ is unrounded; ㅜ is rounded. Say pairs: 크-쿠, 크-쿠. Then `그` (that) versus `구` (nine).
Record both pairs and listen back with headphones. This self-check catches what your ear will not.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (0.3).** You read the full vowel chart from memory, and your recording of 어/오 and 크/쿠 is distinguishable by a native speaker or by a language-exchange partner.

items.text: Every syllable is `(initial consonant) + vowel + (final consonant)`.
Six shapes: `가` (C+V), `강` (C+V+C), `과` (C+V+V), `아` (ㅇ+V), `안` (ㅇ+V+C), `완` (C+V+V+C).
ㅇ is silent in the initial position and *ng* in the final position.
Stroke order: top-left first, then right, then bottom. Learn it once, correctly.
Write each of the 40 letters ten times, saying the sound aloud.
Write your own name in Hangeul, then a Koreanised version of three friends' names.
Write ten words from dictation given by a text-to-speech voice.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (0.4).** You handwrite 20 random syllables from dictation with correct block construction and legible stroke order.

headers: Written letters that collapse into it
rows: ㄷ ㅅ ㅆ ㅈ ㅊ ㅌ ㅎ

items.text: ㄺ → ㄱ before a consonant: 읽다 [익따], 맑다 [막따], 닭 [닥]
ㄻ → ㅁ: 삶 [삼]
ㄼ → ㄹ: 여덟 [여덜], 넓다 [널따]
ㅄ → ㅂ: 값 [갑], 없어요 [업써요]
ㄵ → ㄴ: 앉아요 [안자요]
ㄶ → ㄴ, with the ㅎ dropped: 많아요 [마나요]
A final stop (ㄱ/ㄷ/ㅂ) is never released in Korean — no puff of air at the end. `밥` ends with the lips closed, not with a *p*.
This is the single most audible marker of a foreign accent. Practise stopping the sound in your mouth.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (0.5).** Given any batchim word, you state its seven-sound collapse without a reference, and your recording of 밥/밤/밥 does not release the final.

items.text: This is the most frequent rule in the language. At normal speed, words bleed into each other constantly.
Drill: read 30 two-syllable words where the second begins with ㅇ, applying liaison every time.

modules.title: Aspiration (격음화): ㅎ fuses with a stop

elements.text: ㄱ/ㄷ/ㅂ + ㄱ/ㄷ/ㅂ/ㅅ/ㅈ → tensed.
ㄱ/ㄷ/ㅂ + ㄴ/ㅁ → ㅇ/ㄴ/ㅁ.
ㄴ + ㄹ or ㄹ + ㄴ → [ㄹㄹ].

**The sentence that identifies a beginner.** `괜찮아요` said as *gwaen-chan-a-yo*, with a full ㅎ, is understood — and immediately placed. Say [괜차나요]. Record yourself until it sounds like one word, not four syllables.

**Module completion gate (0.6).** You read 20 unseen words containing sound changes, state which rule applies to each, and your spoken version matches the rule. You can list all seven rules from memory.

items.text: Korean is syllable-timed, not stress-timed. Every syllable gets roughly equal duration; do not crush unstressed syllables the way English does.
Consequence: Korean speech sounds *flatter and faster* than English to a learner, and your English rhythm sounds *lumpy* to a Korean.
Korean uses pitch at the phrase level, not the word level: a rise at the end of a question, a fall at the end of a statement.
Long vowels carry emotional weight: `네~` (yes, drawn out) signals hesitation or disbelief.
There is no lexical tone — pitch does not change word meaning, but it changes *attitude*, which is where misunderstanding lives.

rows: slight rise on each, fall on last

elements.text: **Module completion gate (0.7).** You shadow a 60-second native clip and your recording has the same contour shape — checked visually on a pitch track or by comparing lengths of matched phrases.

items.text: Take a 100-syllable passage, read aloud, time it, divide.
Count errors separately. A fast read with wrong sound rules is not progress.
Start with syllable charts, then word lists, then short sentences, then a paragraph of a children's book.
Read *novel* text every session — re-reading the same passage inflates speed without building decoding.
Read aloud, always. Silent reading at this stage trains nothing.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (0.8).** 60 syllables per minute on unseen text at 98% rule accuracy, measured three days in a row.

modules.title: Dictation as a test of perception

items.text: Dictate 20 words per session from an audio source, in Hangeul.
Mark every miss. Group the misses: was it a consonant, a vowel, a batchim, or a sound rule?
The group with the most misses is your training target for the next session.
Pass 1 blind; pass 2 sentence-by-sentence dictation; pass 3 compare and mark.
Re-listen to the missed spots immediately, three times, before moving on.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (0.9).** 20-word dictation at 95% accuracy, with misses classified by cause rather than simply corrected.

sections.title: Level 0 assessment
sections.objective: **Level 0 completion rule.** If you can read quickly but a native speaker cannot transcribe your speech, you have completed a decoding course, not this level. Repeat 0.6–0.9 until the corpus passes.

elements.text: **Objective.** Produce a recorded, reviewable corpus that proves the level's outcome — not a claim that you "know the alphabet".

items.text: **The alphabet corpus.** You record all 40 letters, isolated, in a single take, with no reading from a list you can see mid-recording.
**The minimal-pair corpus.** Ten triplets (가/카/까 and nine others) recorded twice, with a 2-second gap.
**The sound-rule corpus.** Twenty sentences, each containing at least one sound-change rule, recorded at natural speed.
**The reading corpus.** Three unseen passages of 100+ syllables, read aloud, timed, with the time and syllable count written down.
**The dictation log.** Ten sessions of 20 words, with accuracy per session and a running list of your recurring phoneme errors.
**The self-assessment.** One paragraph, written, naming your three weakest sounds and the drill you used for each.

sections.title: How a Korean sentence is built

items.text: The verb is always last. `저는 밥을 먹어요.` — *I rice eat.*
Everything else can move, because particles mark the role, not the position.
Modifiers come before what they modify: `맛있는 밥` — *delicious rice*.
Consequence for English speakers: you must hold the sentence open until the end. Practise by starting with the verb in mind.
Particles attach directly, with no space: `밥을`, not `밥 을`.
Particles can be dropped in speech and are *never* dropped in formal writing.

sections.title: The copula and the two "to be"s

items.text: `이에요` after a consonant, `예요` after a vowel. This is the most common beginner error in the language.
Negative: `아니에요` — *it is not*. Also `-이/가 아니에요`.
There is no separate adjective "to be" — Korean uses 이다 for identity and 있다/없다 for existence.
Korean has no verb "to have". You say *"time exists"*: `시간이 있어요`.
`있어요` = there is / I have. `없어요` = there isn't / I don't have.
This structure explains the entire 있다/없다 word family: 맛있다/맛없다, 재미있다/재미없다, 의미있다/의미없다.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (1.2).** You produce 이에요/예요 correctly in 20 out of 20 cases, and you can say five things you have and five you don't without using a word for "have".

sections.title: The verb: dictionary form, stem, and classes

items.text: Dictionary form ends in **-다**: 가다, 먹다, 하다.
The **stem** is the dictionary form minus 다: 가, 먹, 하.
All endings attach to the stem. The dictionary form is a citation form, never used in speech except in writing and in the plain-style declarative.

rows: conjugate like verbs but do not take imperatives or progressives
irregular in form, not in meaning
behave like verbs, but 있다 as "have" takes 이/가

elements.text: **The trap:** Korean adjectives are verbs. `예뻐요` is a complete sentence — *she is pretty*. There is no "to be" inserted. English speakers add one for months.
**Module completion gate (2.1).** You classify 30 given verbs into action/descriptive, and write the stem of each.

items.text: `추워요` (it is cold) → `추웠어요` (it was cold).
`맛있어요` → `맛있었어요`.
Past adjectives are how you describe a completed experience: `정말 재미있었어요` — *it was really fun*.

Past form: -ㄹ 거였어요 = *was going to*.
`제가 할게요` — *I'll do it* (because you asked, or as a promise).

items.text: This distinction is not optional. Using 안 when you mean 못 sounds like stubbornness.
안 and 못 go immediately before the verb, never before the object: `밥을 안 먹어요` ✓, `안 밥을 먹어요` ✗.
With 하다 verbs, the 안 goes before 하다: `공부 안 해요`.
Past negation is formed on the tense: 안 갔어요, 못 갔어요, 가지 않았어요, 가지 못했어요.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (2.5).** Twenty sentences negated both ways, with 안/못 chosen correctly and the placement never wrong.

items.text: After a consonant 을, after a vowel 를.
Only transitive verbs take it.
Memorise verbs with their frame: `밥을 먹다`, not `먹다`.
Marks what the sentence is *about*, and often contrasts.
`저는 학생이에요` — *as for me, I'm a student*.
It can replace 이/가 or 을/를 in the same slot: `밥은 먹어요` — *as for rice, I do eat it*.
Marks the doer or the bearer of a state, and signals *this is the answer to the question*.
`누가 왔어요?` → `민수 씨가 왔어요.` (not 는)
`비가 와요` — new information, no contrast.

elements.text: **Do not try to master this at L2.** Learn the five situations above, and let the rest come from exposure between L2 and L7. Fluency in 은/는 vs 이/가 is a late-stage skill, and no amount of rule-reading replaces hearing 1,000 examples.

items.text: **에 vs 에서.** Movement toward or existence at a place → 에. An action performed there → 에서.
**만 vs 밖에.** Both mean "only", but 밖에 always requires a negative verb: `물밖에 없어요`.
**하고 vs 와/과.** Same meaning; 하고 is spoken and can be used with any noun, 와/과 is written and more formal.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (2.7).** 25 sentences with particles blanked out, 22+ correct, with the reason stated for each.

items.text: **Exceptions (regular):** 입다 → 입어요, 잡다 → 잡아요, 좁다 → 좁아요, 씹다 → 씹어요.
**Exceptions:** 받다 → 받아요, 닫다 → 닫아요, 믿다 → 믿어요.
**Exceptions:** 웃다 → 웃어요, 벗다 → 벗어요.
**Exception:** 따르다 → 따라요.
Rule: if the preceding syllable has ㅏ/ㅗ, take -아요; otherwise -어요.
ㄹ drops before ㄴ, ㅂ, ㅅ endings: 살다 → 사세요 (not 살으세요), 알다 → 아는 (not 알는), 만들다 → 만드세요.

`-(으)ㄹ 수 없다` — there is no way.
`못` — I personally cannot, right now.

sections.title: Clause linking I: and, but, so

items.text: Attaches to the stem with no tense: 먹**고**, 가**고**, 하**고**.
Tense appears only on the final verb: `밥을 먹고 학교에 갔어요`.
It sequences, it does not cause. `비가 오고 추워요` — it rains and (also) it's cold.
`비싸지만 좋아요` — it's expensive but I like it.
Can attach to past stems: `갔지만`.
The most versatile connector in the language, and the last one learners acquire.
Background: `지금 바쁜데요…` — *I'm busy right now (so…)*
Contrast: `한국어는 어려운데 재미있어요`.
Softening a request: `죄송한데요, 다시 말씀해 주시겠어요?`
Conjugation: verb stem + 는데; descriptive stem + -(으)ㄴ데; past + -았/었는데.

rows: **cannot** be followed by an imperative or a proposal
reason the listener should accept; discovery

items.text: `비가 와서 못 갔어요` ✓ (statement)
`비가 오니까 우산을 가져가세요` ✓ (imperative — only 니까 works)
`비가 와서 우산을 가져가세요` ✗ (grammatically wrong)
Second use of -니까: discovery. `가 보니까 사람이 없었어요` — *I went and found nobody there.*

items.text: -아/어 보다 — try: 먹어 봤어요 (I've tried it).
-고 싶다 — want: 가고 싶어요.
-고 싶어하다 — third person: 그 사람은 가고 싶어해요. You cannot use 싶다 about someone else's inner state.

items.text: Time clauses take tense only where the time reference differs from the main clause: `비가 왔을 때 집에 있었어요` (it rained, I was home — both past).
`-면` takes no tense at all: 비가 오면, never 비가 왔으면 (that would be counterfactual, a different pattern at L10).

items.text: Note the collision: `-(으)ㄴ` is past for verbs and present for adjectives.
`-던` = used to, or was in the middle of: `내가 살던 집` — the house I used to live in.
`어제 만난 사람이 선생님이에요` — the person I met yesterday is a teacher.
Korean puts the whole relative clause before the noun, with no "who/which". Long modifiers are the main reason reading comprehension slows at intermediate level.

items.text: All three operate at once. A sentence can be simultaneously subject-honorific, object-honorific, and hearer-polite.

items.text: Transcribe 60 seconds, score it, and record the number. Every session. The curve is the point.
Classify every miss: **phoneme** (didn't hear the sound), **contraction** (didn't recognise the form), **lexical** (didn't know the word), **speed** (lost the thread).
The classification tells you what to study. A phoneme problem is a pronunciation problem; a lexical problem is a vocabulary problem; they need different fixes.
60% of your listening time should be **material you understand 70–90% of** — the comprehension zone.
40% should be **material you understand 40–70% of** — the stretch zone.
Material you understand 100% of is entertainment, not practice. That is fine, but it does not count.

items.text: **Learn to recognise, not to imitate.** A learner affecting a Busan accent badly is worse than a learner speaking standard Korean clearly.
Expect to meet 경상 intonation in dramas, in Busan, and in a large share of variety television.
The practical rule: understand the dialect, produce the standard, and never mock either.

levels.title: READING AND WRITING FOUNDATIONS
levels.goal: Read a news brief and a short story with 90% comprehension; write a 300-word diary, a formal email, and a message thread — each in the correct register, with correct spacing.

dashboard.core tools: A news app, graded readers, a notebook, a tutor for corrections
dashboard.main project: **`text-lab`** — a reading log, a diary, an email, and an error taxonomy
dashboard.final outcome: 90% comprehension of a news brief; 300 words of your own prose with ≤ 5 errors; correct spacing and register.

rows: read the first sentence of each paragraph, then the last paragraph
look for numbers, names, and Sino-Korean content words
sentence by sentence, with a dictionary

items.text: Most learners read everything in close-reading mode, which is slow and exhausting. Practise all three deliberately.
A news brief should be skimmed first, then scanned for the who/what/when, then close-read only the paragraph that matters.
Set a threshold: at 90% known words, keep going and infer. At 70%, look up.
Infer from three cues: the Sino-Korean morphemes, the particle pattern, and the sentence position.
`그 회사는 신제품을 출시했다` — if you don't know 출시, the particles tell you it is a verb acting on 신제품, and 하다 tells you it is a Sino-Korean noun-verb. That is often enough.

elements.text: Before reading a long sentence, find:

items.text: The **final verb** — it carries tense, register, and negation.
The **subject particle** (이/가/께서) or topic (은/는).
The **object particle** (을/를).
Any **modifier ending** (-는, -(으)ㄴ, -(으)ㄹ) — everything before it is a clause.
The **connector** (-지만, -는데, -아서) — it tells you the relationship to the next clause.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (6.1).** You skim a 300-word news brief in 30 seconds, state its topic in one Korean sentence, then locate three specific facts by scanning.

rows: `정부, 예산 확대` — no ending at all

items.text: Headlines delete verbs: `정부, 내년 예산 10% 확대` — *government, next year's budget 10% expanded*.
They use the comma to replace a topic marker: `서울시, 지하철 요금 인상` — *Seoul city, subway fares to rise*.
`-할 듯`, `-키로`, `-중` are headline-only forms.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (6.2).** Given ten short texts, you identify the type and the register from the first two lines, with 9/10 correct.

rows: Particles attach to the preceding word
할 수 있다 · 할 것 같다 · 먹을 만큼
Auxiliary verbs are separated (attached is permitted)
Numerals and counters are separated (attached is permitted after digits)
Proper names are written as one unit
Compound nouns are written as one unit
이 사람 · 그 책 · 저 집
Units of time and date attach

elements.text: **Module completion gate (6.3).** You correct 25 spacing errors in a supplied text at 90%+ and state the rule for each correction.

sections.title: The written style: -다 and its registers

items.text: The -다 style is the **default for written prose**: diaries, reports, novels, news.
It is not rude. It is not speech. It is the register of the written page, and confusing the two is the most common stylistic error at this level.
Speech uses 해요체/합니다체; writing uses -다; the two are not interchangeable.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (6.4).** You rewrite a spoken paragraph in -다 style, changing every verb, without altering the meaning.

rows: used more sparingly than in English
quotation within a quotation, or emphasis

items.text: No space before punctuation: `갔어요.` not `갔어요 .`
Korean uses fewer commas than English. Where English needs a comma, Korean often uses a particle instead.
Arabic numerals for prices, dates, phone numbers, and statistics: `15,000원`, `2026년 10월 22일`.
Sino-Korean words for small numbers in prose: `세 명`, `두 시간`.
In formal or literary text, numbers under ten are often written in words.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (6.5).** You format a 150-word text with correct punctuation, numeral style, and quotation marks, and it passes a native read without correction.

items.text: Write in -다 style, not 해요체. Diaries are prose.
Five to eight sentences is enough. Daily beats long.
Use only grammar you have *produced* before. A diary is for consolidation, not experimentation.
Add one sentence per entry using a pattern from the current level. This is how new grammar enters production.
Keep every entry. The Day 1 to Day 100 comparison is the most motivating artefact you will have.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (6.6).** Ten consecutive diary entries, 5+ sentences each, in -다 style, with no more than three errors per entry after correction.

modules.title: The ten phrases that do the work

items.text: `다름이 아니라` — the thing is (soft opener)
`문의드리고 싶은 것이 있습니다` — I'd like to ask about something
`혹시 가능하실까요?` — would it by any chance be possible?
`바쁘시겠지만` — I know you're busy, but
`확인 부탁드립니다` — please check / confirm
`회신 부탁드립니다` — please reply
`이해해 주시면 감사하겠습니다` — I'd be grateful if you understood
`불편을 드려 죄송합니다` — sorry for the inconvenience
`잘 부탁드립니다` — I look forward to working with you
`___ 드림` — from ___ (the closing signature)

modules.title: The three registers of a message

elements.text: **Module completion gate (6.7).** You write a formal enquiry email, a professional message, and a casual message thread, and a native speaker finds no register error in any of the three.

items.text: Sentences run to 40+ syllables, with two or three embedded clauses.
The verb is at the end, so the meaning arrives last. You must hold the pieces in working memory.
Free indirect speech puts a character's thoughts in the narrator's grammar, without quotation marks.
Read the same short story twice: once for the plot with a dictionary, once for the sentences without one.
Mark every sentence over 30 syllables. Those are the ones to parse on paper.
Poetry at L6 is recognition, not mastery. Read it aloud for sound; the meaning comes later.
Korean poetry uses inversion (`하늘을 나는 새` reversed as `나는 새, 하늘을`), archaic endings (-하노라, -리라), and line breaks that carry meaning.
One poem per week, read aloud, not analysed.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (6.8).** You read a 1,000-word short story and write a 150-word summary in Korean with 90% comprehension, plus three sentences on the writing style.

items.text: Most abstract vocabulary is Sino-Korean, built from characters you will formally study at L11.
You can already decode a lot of it: 학교 = 學校 (study + school), 전화 = 電話 (electric + speech), 대학 = 大學 (great + study).
Learning the top 100 characters at L11 will multiply your vocabulary by roughly three. For now, notice the pattern: the same syllable carries the same meaning across dozens of words.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (6.9).** Given ten noun roots, you generate the 하다 verb, the 되다 passive, and the -적 adjective where possible, and explain what each suffix does.

levels.title: DISCOURSE AND CONNECTORS
levels.goal: Hold the floor. Say something for five minutes that has a beginning, three reasons, a concession, and an end — in the right register, without the listener having to work to follow you.

dashboard.core tools: Recorder, tutor twice weekly, a Korean debate or discussion podcast
dashboard.main project: **`argument-lab`** — a five-minute argument with a Q&A
dashboard.final outcome: Five minutes of structured speech on an unprepared topic, with six connectors and one concession.

sections.title: The architecture of a Korean answer

rows: signals that a long answer is coming, buys time
the claim, stated early — not at the end
two or three, each with a marker
shows you have considered the other side

items.text: Unlike English academic style, the position comes **early**. A Korean listener who waits 90 seconds for the thesis assumes you do not have one.
The concession is not optional. An answer with no concession reads as naive.
The close restates, it does not add a new point.
Every part has its own ending, and the register has to stay consistent across all five.
The connectives carry much of the meaning, so a wrong one changes the argument, not just the grammar.
Korean discourse is more **listener-oriented**: you signal your direction constantly (`크게 두 가지가 있는데요…`) rather than surprising the listener.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (7.1).** You deliver a 90-second answer using all five parts, labelled out loud ("여기서부터 이유입니다"), and a listener can name your position after hearing it once.

sections.title: Cause and reason: the refined set

rows: reason the listener should accept; discovery
a reason that *occupied* you, usually with a negative result
subject must be the same, present/past only
an unwelcome cause with a bad outcome
because I saw/heard that, so I acted
first person action in the result

modules.title: The three you will actually use

items.text: **-느라고** takes the blame: `전화 받느라고 못 봤어요` — I didn't see it because I was on the phone.
**-는 바람에** assigns an external cause to a bad result: `지하철이 멈추는 바람에 늦었어요`.
**-길래** reports a perceived cause: `맛있어 보이길래 샀어요` — it looked good so I bought it.

elements.text: **The constraint that matters:** -느라고 and -는 바람에 cannot be followed by a request or a command. If you add `-세요`, the sentence collapses. Same restriction as -아/어서, and the same reason: the speaker is reporting, not directing.
**Module completion gate (7.2).** Fifteen cause sentences, each using a *different* pattern, with the nuance explained in one clause.

rows: 네 말이 맞다 해도 문제는 남아요

items.text: `물론 ___지만, 그래도 ___` — of course X, but even so Y. This is the single most useful argumentative structure in Korean.
`-기는 하지만` is the softened version and is what makes you sound reasonable rather than combative.
`-는데도` is *despite*, and it carries frustration. Do not use it about a person in a formal setting.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (7.3).** Ten concessions, each conceding a real point and then contradicting it, delivered to a tutor who argues back.

modules.title: The two that carry the most meaning

items.text: **-았/었더니** combines a past action with a discovery, and the second clause must be a *result you observed*: `전화했더니 안 받더라고요`.
**-(으)ㄹ수록** is a rhetorical favourite: `생각할수록 화가 나요` — the more I think, the angrier I get.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (7.4).** A six-sentence narrative using five different sequence connectors, with no tense error in the subordinate clauses.

rows: It wouldn't be a bad idea

items.text: In Korean professional speech, the stronger the disagreement, the softer the wording. Bluntness is not honesty — it is a register error.
`-것 같아요` is not weakness. It is the default stance of a polite adult expressing an opinion.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (7.5).** You disagree with ten statements, each at a different level of directness, and state which level suits which setting.

rows: 제 생각에는 · 개인적으로는 · 이 문제에 대해
첫째 · 둘째 · 셋째 · 먼저 · 다음으로 · 마지막으로

items.text: Rehearse the skeleton on five different topics. The topics do not matter; the shape does.
The concession is where most learners fall apart, because it requires switching sides for two sentences while keeping the register.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (7.6).** A five-minute argument on a prepared topic, recorded, scored against the skeleton with every part present.

rows: 그 지적은 타당합니다 / 그 부분은 맞습니다
그 얘기도 중요하지만, 제가 말씀드린 건
그 부분은 제가 잘 모르겠습니다. 확인해 보겠습니다

items.text: Do not restart the whole argument when interrupted. Answer the specific objection, then return with `그래서 처음에 말씀드린 것처럼…`.
`그 부분은 제가 잘 모르겠습니다` is a strong answer, not a weak one. Confident ignorance beats invented facts.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (7.7).** You argue a position while a tutor interrupts three times with objections, and you return to your thread each time without restarting.

rows: but, by the way — the commonest turn in speech
kind of, a bit — the universal softener
like, or something — intensifier in slang
now, then — a filler that means nothing

items.text: A silent pause reads as failure; a filled pause reads as thinking. This is the single biggest cheap improvement available at this level.
`약간` and `좀` make almost any sentence sound more natural and less aggressive.
`막` and `완전` belong to casual speech only — using them in a formal setting is a register error, not a vocabulary error.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (7.8).** A three-minute monologue with no dead air over two seconds, using at least eight different markers.

items.text: `아, 그게 아니라` — no, that's not it (the commonest repair)
`다시 말하면` — let me rephrase
`제가 말을 잘못했는데` — I said that badly
`그게 아니라, ___` — it's not that, it's ___
Repairing is a *fluency* behaviour. Learners who never repair sound worse than learners who repair often.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (7.9).** You deliver a two-minute answer containing at least two self-repairs, both smooth enough that the argument does not break.

items.text: Prepare nothing. A partner names a topic; you speak for the target time.
Topics should be ordinary: remote work, learning languages, city versus countryside, social media, university education, AI, food culture, exercise, travel, money.
Record every attempt. The measure is *time sustained without a break longer than three seconds*.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (7.10).** Five minutes on an unprepared topic, recorded, with ≥ 4.5 minutes of speech and no break over three seconds.

items.text: Korean does **not** backshift tense the way English does. `간다고 했어요` = *he said he is going / was going*. The time is carried by the outer verb and the context.
To be explicit: past `갔다고 했어요`, future `갈 거라고 했어요`.
The outer verb can be anything: 말하다, 하다, 생각하다, 믿다, 듣다, 물어보다, 쓰다.

modules.title: The four that carry the most social weight

items.text: **-네요** is the politeness of noticing. Saying `맛있네요` instead of `맛있어요` makes you gracious.
**-잖아요** is a reproach dressed as a reminder. Use it with people you know; it is confrontational with strangers.
**-거든요** ends a topic. It says *this is my reason, and I am not inviting discussion*.
**-기는요** is the correct response to a compliment, and refusing it too firmly is its own error.

levels.title: ADVANCED GRAMMAR PATTERNS
levels.goal: Master the TOPIK Level 4–5 grammar architecture: multi-clause hypothetical conditions, nuanced supposition, regret, inevitability, and concessive constructions. Transition from "correct sentences" to expressing exact degrees of probability, intention, and emotional stance.
levels.prerequisites: Level 9 passed. Clear grasp of quoted speech, formal registers, and intermediate conjunctions.

items.text: Understand `-(으)ㄹ 텐데` as combining future expectation/supposition `-(으)ㄹ 터이다` with background connector `-ㄴ/은/는데`.
Contrast `비가 올 텐데 우산을 가져가세요` (strong anticipation offering advice) with `비가 올 텐데요` (sentence ending expressing concern or presumption).
Drill the past supposition variant: `-았/었을 텐데` (e.g. `많이 피곤했을 텐데 푹 쉬세요`).
Understand `-(으)ㄴ/는 모양이다` as deduction based on observable external signs or evidence.
Contrast with `-나 보다` (informal, intuitive deduction) vs `-(으)ㄴ/는 모양이다` (written/spoken, based on visible cues).
Conjugate correctly across tenses: `-은 모양이다` (past), `-는 모양이다` (present verb), `-(으)ㄴ 모양이다` (adjective), `-(으)ㄹ 모양이다` (imminent future).

items.text: Rank determines register, seating, who speaks first, who pours, and who pays. It is not decoration.

elements.text: Every wrong answer in block D–H is one of these. Learn to recognise them and the section gets dramatically easier.

a statement that is factually in the audio but is not the answer to *this* question

elements.text: **The single most reliable listening rule:** if an option contains `항상`, `절대`, `모두`, or `반드시`, it is wrong unless the speaker literally used that word. The exam writers use absolutes as a trap because they are easy to construct and easy to detect.

elements.text: When you miss something, you get **four seconds** to decide: keep listening or abandon the question. Most candidates lose five questions' worth of points by still processing question 34 while question 35 is playing.

elements.label: The decision rule
elements.value: if you cannot reconstruct the answer from your notes within four seconds of the audio ending, mark a guess and move. A guess is worth 0 or 2. A lost question 35 because you were still on 34 is also 0 or 2 — but you have now lost the option of guessing well.

elements.text: The single most learnable question type on the paper. The inserted sentence must attach to *something* — a pronoun, a repeated noun, or a connector.

elements.text: Do not read them in order. Find the sentence that **cannot** come first — the one that opens with a connector or a pronoun — and build outward from it.
Method:

items.text: Cross out every sentence beginning with a connector. Those are not first.
Find the sentence with a bare noun subject and no back-reference. That is usually first.

levels.title: TRANSLATION AND INTERPRETATION
levels.goal: Move meaning between Korean and one other language without losing the things that make it mean. By the end you can translate a 3,000-word document with a translator's note explaining every hard choice, and perform fifteen minutes of consecutive interpreting from audio you have never heard.
levels.prerequisites: Level 15 complete. In practice: TOPIK 6 level (230+), and — the part that actually matters — you can read a Korean sentence and say what it *does*, not only what it says.

dashboard.core tools: Parallel corpora, a glossary spreadsheet, a recorder, an interpreting tutor, published translations to compare against
dashboard.main project: **`bridge-kit`** — a translation portfolio, a 300-term glossary, and a recorded consecutive performance
dashboard.final outcome: Three translated texts with notes, a 15-minute consecutive interpretation at ≥ 80% content accuracy, and a 300-term glossary.

rows: a correct sentence that reads like a translation

modules.title: The four things that must survive

elements.text: A translation succeeds if these four cross the bridge. They are listed in order of how often they are abandoned.

headers: What it looks like when lost
rows: the facts are wrong — a hard failure, rare
a corporate apology reads like a text message, or a poem reads like a manual
the politeness, the threat, the joke, the reluctance — all gone
the sentence is correct and unreadable; a native would never have written it

elements.text: **The amateur trade:** sacrifice 2, 3, and 4 to preserve 1. **The professional trade:** sacrifice surface form to preserve all four.

modules.title: The unit is the sentence, and sometimes the paragraph

elements.text: Literal translation fails because Korean and English do not share sentence boundaries. A Korean sentence may contain four clauses that English would split into three sentences. A single English sentence may collapse into one Korean clause plus a trailing `-는데`.

elements.label: The rule
elements.value: if you find yourself translating clause by clause and the result is grammatical but strange, the boundary is wrong, not the words.

items.text: Take one paragraph of Korean newspaper prose and one of English newspaper prose on the same event. Compare sentence counts. Notice the ratio.

rows: must be carried by verb choice or context
register is often invisible in English until it is wrong
the humility is lost unless the verb is upgraded
past tense plus a hint of personal witness ("I remember", "I found")
bare past tense that loses the witnessing

elements.text: English requires a subject. Korean drops it. When you translate into Korean, you must decide — every time — whether `you` becomes `너`, `당신`, `여러분`, a title, or nothing at all.

rows: `당신` is confrontational outside arguments and translations
drop the pronoun; let the verb carry it

elements.text: **The rule:** in Korean, `당신` and `너` are *marked*. Their absence is the default. If your Korean translation is full of `당신`, it was translated from English.

items.text: Take ten English sentences containing "you" and translate them into Korean without using `당신` once. Justify each choice.

You can name the register of any Korean passage on sight.

sections.title: Korean into English: three structural problems

elements.text: Korean marks topic (`-은/는`) and subject (`-이/가`) separately. English marks only subject. The consequence: Korean sentences begin with a topic that is not the grammatical subject, and a literal translation produces a sentence with no engine.

elements.label: The method
elements.value: find the `-이/가` phrase. That is your English subject. The `-은/는` phrase becomes the object, the time expression, or the place.

elements.text: Korean drops subjects, objects, and sometimes verbs entirely. English cannot. When you translate, you must *supply* what Korean omitted — and get it wrong about 20% of the time if you are careless.
**The three questions to ask of every clause:**

items.text: Who is doing this?
What are they doing it to?
Is this a new fact or a continuation?

elements.text: If a Korean passage says `그렇게 하기로 했다` with no subject, the answer is in the previous sentence, and you must carry it forward into English.
This is the hardest structural feature of Korean, and the one that makes machine translation fail visibly.

elements.code: 그가 작년에 처음 만났다고 말했던 그 사람이 지금 우리 회사에서 일하고 있다.

elements.text: Everything before `그 사람` is a relative clause stacked onto a noun. English cannot do this. The **unpack-and-rebuild** method:

rows: Find the head noun — here `그 사람`
List the clauses attached to it, in order
Decide which becomes a relative clause, which becomes a separate sentence, which becomes an appositive
Rebuild in English order — usually head noun first, then clauses to the right

elements.label: Result
elements.value: "The man he said he'd first met last year now works at our company." Or, better, split: "He said he'd first met the man last year. That man now works at our company."

elements.text: **Rule of thumb:** a Korean modifier chain longer than three clauses becomes two English sentences. Native English writers do not stack; they serialise.

items.text: Take ten Korean sentences with `-은/는` topics that are not subjects. Translate them with the `-이/가` rule and check against a published translation.
Take five modifier chains of three or more clauses and unpack each into two or three English sentences.

Take a published Korean→English translation of a novel paragraph and back-translate it into Korean. Compare with the original. Note every place the translator chose differently from the source structure.
Ten topic-prominence sentences translated without a single "As for..." construction.
Five modifier chains unpacked, none exceeding two clauses in English.
A back-translation that recovers ≥ 90% of the original's propositions.

sections.title: English into Korean: the harder direction

elements.text: English has `a`, `the`, and zero article. Korean has `이`, `그`, `저`, and — most often — nothing.

rows: first mention takes no determiner; use a counter

elements.label: The rule
elements.value: English articles map to Korean *information structure*, not to Korean words. First mention → no marker or a counter. Second mention → `그`. Generic → bare noun with `-은/는`.

elements.text: English puts relatives to the right of the noun; Korean puts them to the left and without a relative pronoun. This is where machine translation produces Korean that is technically parseable and completely foreign.

rows: "The report that the team submitted last week was rejected."
"Anyone who wants to join should sign up."
"A policy that would help small businesses"

elements.label: Three fixes
elements.value: delete the `그`; choose the correct particle (`-이/가` vs `-은/는`) by information structure; and replace the literal verb with the collocation Koreans actually use (`거절되다` → `반려되다` in a corporate document).

elements.text: English prefers passive in formal writing; Korean prefers active with a plural subject, or the `-어지다` / `-게 되다` construction, or an impersonal noun.

rows: "It was decided that the meeting would be postponed."

elements.text: After a first draft, run four checks in this order. They catch about 80% of translationese.

rows: delete most; Korean repeats the noun or drops it
does every `-은/는` mark a topic, and every `-이/가` a new fact?
swap the ones that are decorative
is the verb a translation of an English verb, or the verb a Korean would use?
does every sentence end the way this register ends?
`-입니다` in a report, `-한다` in an editorial

elements.label: The 10-term rule
elements.value: if a document uses a technical term more than ten times, it goes in the glossary before you translate sentence one.

it is often the schoolbook version, not the industry version
**Industry usage** (the client's own documents, competitor sites, trade press)

proof that the term functions in context

sections.title: Sight translation and the timed pressure of the booth

elements.text: You cannot revise, you cannot search, and the audience hears your thinking. The skill is **chunking**: read a clause, hold it, say it, move on — while reading the next clause with the other eye.

headers: Why it is separate from translation
rows: you must break the sentence *before* you know how it ends
a hard term must be handled without a pause
hesitation reads as incompetence, even when the content is right

elements.text: You are usually given 1–3 minutes with the text before speaking. Spend it like this:

rows: read the title, the first sentence, and the last sentence — that is the argument
scan for numbers, names, and terms — mark them, because they cannot be improvised
read the first two paragraphs closely; the rest you will read cold

elements.text: When you hit a term you do not know, you have three options, in this order of preference:

items.text: **Circumlocute**: "a type of chemical used in semiconductor cleaning" — say what it does.
**Preserve and move**: say the term in the source language and continue — legitimate in a technical setting.
**Flag**: "the exact term here is technical; I'll come back to it" — and do come back.

elements.label: Never
elements.value: invent a term that sounds plausible. A wrong drug name or a wrong legal term is a real-world harm.

elements.text: **Read the target text alone on pass 2.** If you read source and target side by side you will see what you meant to write, not what is there.
A proper note has four parts, in this order:

"a corporate apology, addressed to customers, formal in both languages"
the three to five hard choices and why

elements.text: **Why the note matters more than it looks:** a client who can see your reasoning can defend the translation to their own boss. A translator who never states a decision gets overruled on style by someone who has not read the source.

levels.title: NATIVE-ADJACENT FLUENCY
levels.goal: Be mistaken for a native for a sustained stretch — not on the phone for thirty seconds, and not because you said one idiom correctly, but for twenty minutes in a conversation you did not prepare.  **What this level is not.** It is not accent elimination. Some learners reach near-native prosody and some never do, and the difference is mostly age of onset and ear. Accent is the least important thing in this level and the thing learners obsess over most. **Being mistaken for native and being native-adjacent are different targets, and only the second one is required here.**

dashboard.core tools: Three native friends who will tell you the truth, a recorder you actually use, Korean-language media consumed for pleasure
dashboard.main project: **`fluency-proof`** — a 60-minute unprepared talk, a 3,000-word short story, and a native-blind test
dashboard.final outcome: Sixty minutes of speech with no preparation, a short story a Korean would finish reading, and a twenty-minute conversation in which the other person did not know.

modules.title: The five things that still mark you

elements.text: These are what a Korean hears as foreign, in roughly descending order of how often they occur. None of them are grammatical.

rows: every sentence has a subject, verb, and object
drop pronouns; let the verb carry the meaning
Korean is not stress-timed; the phrase carries the beat
too clear, too slow, no elision
saying the obvious, because you fear being misunderstood
trust the listener; cut a third

elements.text: The only honest measurement is this: **a Korean who does not know you talks to you for twenty minutes and does not ask where you are from.**
It is an unreliable test — a polite Korean may not ask even if they suspect. So use the four-probe version:

rows: a stranger on the phone does not detect you (no visual cues)
you follow a three-way conversation with overlapping speech and interruptions
you laugh before the punchline lands, because you saw it coming
a Korean corrects your Korean as if you were a native who misspoke, not a learner who erred

elements.text: **The fourth probe is the real one.** When a Korean says `그거 아니고...` rather than `외국인이시죠?`, you have crossed. It means they have stopped modelling you as a learner.

elements.text: **Why this matters more than it looks:** a learner who speaks with textbook clarity sounds *careful*. Careful is the signal. Koreans reduce because the information is redundant; if you do not reduce, you sound like you are reading aloud.
Korean is a **phrase-timed** language with a light pitch accent that is not lexical, plus a final contour that carries politeness.

modules.title: 아재개그, and why bad puns matter

elements.text: 아재개그 is a genre of pun so weak it becomes funny through the telling. It is a social ritual: the teller knows it is bad, the listener groans, and the groan is the point.

elements.label: Why you should learn three of them
elements.value: not because they are funny, but because deploying one is a recognised move in Korean social humour. It signals that you are *inside* the game rather than observing it. A foreigner who tells a bad 아재개그 and waits for the groan has made a cultural joke about the culture, which is a different and better joke than a good pun.

rows: the teller reacts *with* the room; deadpan is less common than shared laughter
you must recover fast, and self-deprecatingly
seniority matters — a junior jokes *at* themselves, not at the senior

elements.text: **The social constraint that surprises learners:** humour in Korean workplaces is often used to *soften a request or a criticism*, not to entertain. Reading a joke as entertainment when it is actually an instruction is a real professional hazard.

The hardest part is not producing jokes; it is laughing at the right moment. Korean humour is often carried by **tone and timing rather than content** — the same sentence is funny or serious depending on the lengthening of the final syllable.

elements.label: The habit
elements.value: when a group laughs and you did not, do not ask "what did they say". Ask "what was the *turn*". The joke is usually in the last three syllables, said slowly.

elements.text: Underlying logic: the relationship survives the message. Direct refusal, direct criticism, and direct disagreement all risk the relationship, so they are routed through implication. This is not dishonesty — it is a different contract about what a sentence is *for*.

sections.title: Slang, youth language, and the decay curve

elements.text: Slang is the highest-risk vocabulary in the language for a foreign learner, because **getting it slightly wrong is worse than not using it at all.** A Korean who uses last year's slang to a twenty-year-old sounds like a visiting relative. A foreign learner who does it sounds like a textbook that has been taught by an older textbook.

elements.label: The rule
elements.value: learn to *understand* fifty slang terms and *use* five. Comprehension is safe; production is a minefield.

elements.text: These are recent, widely understood, and mostly stable enough to be recognisable for a while. Glosses are functional, not dictionary definitions.
Before you use any slang term, ask three questions:

rows: Would a 25-year-old use it without irony?
it is dated — understand it, don't produce it

Would you use it in front of a client?

elements.label: The professional rule
elements.value: in any setting where money or hierarchy is involved, use no slang. `워라밸` and `N잡러` are borderline-acceptable workplace vocabulary; `쌉가능` is not.

elements.text: Slang decays at roughly five to seven years; some terms persist as "older person's slang", which is worse than disappearing.

rows: `눈치`, `정` — these are not slang, they are Korean

elements.label: Maintenance

modules.title: Why reference is harder than vocabulary

elements.text: A Korean sentence can contain a reference that carries half the meaning and none of the information. `요즘 애들은` presupposes a theory of generations. `우리 때는` presupposes a shared past. Neither can be looked up, because neither is a definition.
Koreans use generational labels as arguments. Each one carries a claim about who is responsible for what.

elements.text: **How to handle these:** use them to *read*, not to *speak*. Saying `MZ세대는...` in a room of people in their twenties is a known way to sound like a consultant. Saying it in an essay about workplace conflict is normal.
Every educated Korean has these as background. You do not need depth; you need recognition and the correct emotional register.

modules.title: Why an hour is a different skill

elements.text: Five minutes is a set piece. Sixty minutes is a *structure*. The failure mode is not grammar — it is running dry at minute twenty-two and then repeating yourself for forty minutes.

elements.label: The arithmetic
elements.value: at a normal speaking rate, sixty minutes is roughly 9,000–12,000 Korean syllables. You need enough *content*, not enough *words*.

elements.text: A long talk runs on four tanks, drawn in order, and each one refills the last.

elements.label: The refill trick
elements.value: every time you feel the tank emptying, return to a *story*, not to abstraction. Stories are inexhaustible because detail is infinite. Abstractions are finite and you will hit the wall.

elements.text: What holds an hour together is not vocabulary but signposting. Have these automatic.
**Buying time is a skill, not a failure.** `잠깐 생각을 정리해 보면` said calmly reads as deliberation. Silence with a searching expression reads as a vocabulary gap. The difference is entirely in the phrase.

modules.title: Why fiction is the hardest test

elements.text: Non-fiction lets you use the registers you have drilled. Fiction requires **voice** — a narrator whose sentences are consistent, whose omissions are deliberate, and whose dialogue sounds like people rather than like examples.

It also requires the thing that Korean short fiction does better than almost any other tradition: **restraint**. The Korean short story is often built around what is not said, and around a situation that does not resolve.

levels.title: TEACHING AND LIFELONG MASTERY
levels.goal: Two things. First, be able to *explain* Korean — which is the deepest test of understanding there is, and the only one that exposes the gaps that fluency hides. Second, build the regime that keeps the language alive for decades, because the single most common outcome of reaching an advanced level is losing it by neglect.  **Why teaching is the final level.** A user of a language can be excellent and still not know why anything works. A teacher must be able to say what the rule is, when it bends, which exceptions matter, and why the learner's version was wrong rather than merely different. That knowledge cannot be faked, and building it fixes things fluency never touched.

**When does it not apply?** (constraints, register, exceptions)

elements.text: If you can only answer question one, you are a native speaker with a textbook, which is not a teacher.

You will be worse than a native Korean teacher at explaining Korean culture and worse than a trained teacher at classroom management. What you have that neither has: **you did this recently, consciously, and from outside** — which means you remember what it was like not to know, and you know which explanations actually worked on you.
**Teach from that.** Your comparative advantage is not authority. It is the memory of confusion.

elements.text: **The rule of two:** two corrections per session, chosen deliberately, marked in your notes, revisited next time. A learner who fixes two things a week fixes a hundred things a year. A learner corrected on everything fixes nothing, because none of it is retained.

Research on corrective feedback is consistent on one point: **frequency of correction predicts uptake, and frequency of praise predicts willingness to speak.** You need both, and you need them in a ratio a learner can feel — roughly three positive or neutral interactions for every correction.

elements.text: **Pass: 70% overall, with no component below 55%.** **Native judgement required regardless of score.** If a bilingual professional would not put their name on the translation, the phase is not complete — even at 85%.

**The brief.** There is no exam above TOPIK 6, so the capstone is the invention of one: a panel of three native speakers who do not know you well, a day of performance, and a verdict you cannot appeal.  **Why it is called the Passing.** Because the thing being tested is not knowledge. It is whether you can pass — as a colleague, as a conversation partner, as a writer, as a teacher — in front of people with no reason to be generous.
